name: glanceswitch
tagline: A keyboard-driven quick switcher that puts your apps, windows or workspaces one glance and one keystroke away.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Switcher utilities live or die on hotkey handling, a fast fuzzy filter and an overlay that appears in under 100ms, all of which an agent can produce in a session. There is no network, no shared data and no reason anyone else needs to be using your build for it to work. The hard parts are platform permissions and the last 10 percent of polish: focus stealing, multi-monitor placement, icon caching, behaving on wake from sleep. Details on this specific product are thin, so if it turns out to lean on cross-device sync or per-app deep integrations the answer slides toward kinda. As a personal tool for your own machine, this is a yes.
coreLoopDIY: A global hotkey pops a borderless overlay that fuzzy-filters open windows and installed apps and focuses or launches the selection on Enter.
requirements: Node 20 and a desktop OS you control
Accessibility and screen recording permissions on macOS for window enumeration and focus
Willingness to fight your window manager for a frameless always-on-top overlay
whatYouLose: Sub-100ms cold start and the tuned animation that makes a switcher feel invisible instead of laggy
Correct behavior on every edge case: multiple monitors, fullscreen apps, virtual desktops, sleep and wake
Signed, notarized, auto-updating builds instead of a dev-mode window you relaunch by hand
Any sync of settings or hotkeys across machines
Someone else's opinionated defaults, which in switcher land is most of the product
moatNotes: The moat here is milliseconds and edge cases, not data. That is real, but it is also the kind of moat you can decide you do not care about.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a switcher you use forty times a day is judged on feel, and feel is the part that takes months of tuning rather than an afternoon of scaffolding. Paying a few dollars to skip permission prompts, monitor bugs and a homemade overlay that flickers on wake is a rational trade for most people. The DIY version is genuinely usable, it just never quite disappears into the background the way a polished one does.
notes: Local utility, no network, no lock-in: the only thing standing between you and a clone is your patience for macOS accessibility permissions.
prompt:
Build a local, keyboard-driven quick switcher desktop app. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Electron with TypeScript and Vite, plain React for the overlay UI, plain CSS. No UI framework, no state library, no database.

Behavior:
1. Register a global hotkey (default Alt+Space, configurable) that shows a frameless, transparent, always-on-top, centered overlay window of about 640x420, with no dock or taskbar presence.
2. The overlay is a single text input plus a result list. Typing filters instantly.
3. Results come from two sources, merged and ranked: currently open windows (title plus owning app) and installed applications. On macOS enumerate apps from /Applications and ~/Applications and use a small helper for open windows; on Linux use wmctrl if present; degrade gracefully to apps-only if window enumeration fails, and say so in the UI.
4. Ranking: fuzzy subsequence match on name and title, boosted by a per-item use counter persisted in a JSON file under app userData. Most recently used wins ties.
5. Enter focuses the window or launches the app. Escape hides the overlay. Up/Down and Ctrl+N/Ctrl+P move the selection. Clicking a row selects it.
6. Cache app icons and names on first run, refresh in the background on show, never block paint on enumeration.
7. Keep the overlay window created and hidden between invocations so show is instant. Do not create it on demand.

Also include: a small preferences window for the hotkey and for toggling window enumeration, launch-at-login via app.setLoginItemSettings, and a tray icon with Preferences and Quit.

Out of scope: file search, web search, calculators, plugins, sync, mobile, auto-update, code signing.

Deliverables: working repo, npm run dev and npm run build, README documenting required macOS Accessibility permission and how to grant it, and a KNOWN-ISSUES.md listing multi-monitor and wake-from-sleep caveats you did not solve. Config and state in JSON under userData. Any secrets, if you somehow need one, go in .env.
